entries.title: The Work of Math in the Age of Artificial Reproduction
entries.summary: There are seven questions in pure mathematics deemed important enough by the Clay Mathematics Institute, a nonprofit foundation devoted to “furthering the beauty, power and universality of mathematical thought,” that each of their solutions carries a prize of $1 million. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
There are seven questions in pure mathematics deemed important enough by the Clay Mathematics Institute, a nonprofit foundation devoted to “furthering the beauty, power and universality of mathematical thought,” that each of their solutions carries a prize of $1 million. To date only one of these “Millennium Prize Problems,” as the foundation calls them, has been settled: the Poincaré conjecture. A problem in topology—the study of the properties of shapes that survive stretching and bending—it had been “open” for almost a century before it was proved in the early 2000s by the Russian mathematician Grigory Perelman. But on September 8 OpenAI announced that it had settled a second Millennium Problem. While Perelman had turned down the prize money (as well as mathematics’ most prestigious award, the Fields Medal), rejecting both the notion of celebrity for mathematicians and the conceit that credit should be given to him alone, OpenAI issued a press release. The company’s claim, still awaiting the community’s judgment, concerns the solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations.

Equations are compact symbolic expressions that say that two ways of doing something mathematically are equivalent. They are most interesting when there is something unknown involved, in which case a “solution” is the thing you “plug in” to give you the same thing “on both sides.” In this way, an equation gives you an indirect description of a mathematical object. A familiar one is x² + 4 = 5x, which says, “I am thinking of a number that, when I multiply it by itself and add four, is the same as if I just multiplied it by 5.” Only two numbers fit that description: 1 and 4.

A differential equation is an equation about change. In a simple example, it might be about some quantity changing with respect to time. Think of an infant on a playground swing. You launch her from a height and let gravity take over. She goes back and forth; at the highest points she stops for an instant and then travels back. As she moves back and forth her position relative to the center changes over time. She starts from “0,” then goes maybe a few feet behind, then a few feet ahead, and the corresponding numbers swing from positive to negative. Her acceleration also changes, and the farther out she swings the more strongly she is pulled back toward the center. The relationship between the position and acceleration can be encoded as a differential equation (including a mathematical caveat for air resistance). But here a solution is not a number. It is a record of the swing’s position at every moment, what mathematicians call a function. Drawn as a graph, it looks like a run of Formula-1 S-curves tapering toward a finish line.

When the unknown quantity depends on changes in more than one other factor—say both where you look and when (space and time)—then we have a partial differential equation. The traditional wave equation is one famous example with many applications. It even applies to a guitar string, when we consider the up-down displacement of any point on the string from rest. Here the wave equation encodes a relationship between that displacement and changes in the position on the string and the time since plucking it. At the beginning and end, where the string is pinned down, there is no movement. The closer you get to where you plucked it, the more it goes back and forth. Here the solutions include the famous sinusoidal waves that we associate with harmonics. Analogous equations can be written for a drumhead or the surface of a pond.

The Navier-Stokes equations, named for the French engineer Claude-Louis Navier and the Cambridge mathematician and physicist George Stokes, are also partial differential equations. They are foundational to a mathematical description of liquids and gases, and as such are essential to the study of fluid dynamics. A solution has two components: one function that gives the velocity of the fluid at every point in space and time (the “velocity field”) and another that gives the pressure at every point in space and time.

Like any good math problem, these have some conditions. The fluid is incompressible, meaning that whatever flows into a region must flow out. There is a viscosity parameter that gauges the “stickiness” of the fluid (molasses has high viscosity, WD-40 has low viscosity). Of course the fluid need not just sit there (it could, but that would be simple to describe), so we allow for an external force to generate the action. It can be strong and even violent in its effect, but it must be mathematically (and quintessentially) “smooth” throughout. Even the geometry of the container is idealized: we imagine that the fluid flows throughout three-dimensional space. No corners, no rough surfaces, free and unfettered, driven only by perfectly smooth Platonic paddlers.

Advertisement

The mathematician Leonhard Euler is generally credited as the first (in 1757) to formulate equations that model how fluid flows. The Euler equations are simply Navier-Stokes equations without viscosity. Euler later applied them to derive a model for blood flowing through arteries. In the early 1800s Navier tried to build on the Euler equations to create a more detailed description that accounted for viscosity. By the 1840s Stokes had cleaned up this attempt to give us the equations we use today.

Navier-Stokes is so fundamental—and provides such a good model of fluid dynamics—that we live its success every day. It underlies the mathematical modeling necessary for tasks ranging from weather prediction to airplane design. It is applied mathematics at its best: terse yet precise, as simple as possible, but not simpler, as Einstein would say. Its simplicity belies the difficulty of understanding the full range of what it encodes—that is, the full range of its possible solutions.

What makes the solutions especially tricky to figure out is a subtlety in their description: there is one “term,” like a phrase in a stanza or a chord in a measure, accounting for the fact that any flowing fluid at once moves with the current and makes the current. Think of a river. There are fast places and slow places, straight stretches and eddies. A leaf on the river—or leaves scattered about the river—materialize the velocity field. But we also have to remember that there is water moving through all this, effectively a continuum of infinitesimal packets of water both making up the current and riding the current. How fast and in what direction the water is moving therefore interacts with how the current varies from place to place. This gives the equations what mathematicians call a nonlinearity. It is also the source of turbulence, both mathematically and—for those trying to solve the equations—analytically.

For generations nobody could say whether the equations, starting from a perfectly smooth flow, could produce a point at which, in a finite time, the speed of the fluid becomes infinite. Such a “singularity” or “blow-up” would be a system spinning wildly out of control—and since real water cannot move infinitely fast, it would be the place where the equations stop describing the world. Resolving this lacuna is the Millenium Problem. It doesn’t keep us from applying Navier-Stokes in real-world settings, but it has been a nagging gap in the landscape of our mathematical knowledge. It now seems that we know the answer: despite the relatively innocuous-sounding assumptions, blow-ups can occur. The coincidence of simplicity of description and complexity of behavior is amazing, and surprising.

The story of the problem’s solution has by now been widely reported. In mid-August the NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and his collaborator Levent Alpöge, an employee of Anthropic, found a blow-up for a version of the Euler equations. Buckmaster and Alpöge built on the work of two Spanish mathematicians, Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa, who (building in turn on Martínez-Zoroa’s dissertation work) had by 2023 found a strategy to create a singularity out of an “infinite cascade” of nonsingular solutions, each one amplifying the effects of the previous ones. Buckmaster and Alpöge also used a range of large language models in their work. Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa used none.

OpenAI has a group of researchers studying the use of the company’s models for math research. While Alpöge and Buckmaster were working to finish a write-up of their solution, OpenAI heard rumors that significant progress had been made toward solving two of the open Millennium Problems. Not knowing which two, but now aware that the solutions were close, the company presumably saw an opportunity for their own research and business efforts. They put their latest, unreleased model to work on all six problems, along with some easier but still important warm-ups. Among those warm-ups were the Euler equations. After around fifty hours of compute time by nearly one hundred AI agents, they too came up with a solution that produced a singularity, which gave them confidence to go all-in on attacking Navier-Stokes.

To this task, by their estimation, they dedicated “on the order of” ten thousand agents. The agents were given the new Euler proof and centuries’ worth of published mathematical work. They very well may also have benefited from the residue of several years of mathematicians’ interactions with OpenAI’s wide range of tools. This swarm of agents was set up in such a way that they could efficiently share their findings among themselves—and share they did. They “talked” to one another for eighty-eight hours, generating 2.7 million messages—130 billion tokens of output, the equivalent of about several hundred thousand books of scratch work.

Advertisement

OpenAI’s human mathematicians oversaw the process, periodically using a second model to consolidate the most promising threads and feed them back. OpenAI has not said how much computing the effort consumed, but outside estimates put it at several hundred thousand GPU-hours, which translate to roughly the amount of electricity it takes to power a town for the four or so days that the model ran. Eventually the problem fell. The machine’s work still needs to be verified by humans, but initial assessments suggest that the problem has been settled.

The controversy over these results began as OpenAI strategized about how to make them public. The night before the company’s announcement, Buckmaster made a post on Mastodon sharing his and Alpöge’s achievements, including the Euler result. He included links to preprint versions of the work as well as supporting materials, the latter of which included a “Lean-4” version of their work that enables a computer program to verify their proof.

Also attached was a document giving his version of the timeline and process, crediting the early work of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa (whom Buckmaster recommended for a Fields Medal) and claiming that he and Alpöge had also made significant progress toward resolving the Millennium Problem. He apologized for the somewhat unpolished nature of their write-ups (“AI slop” is how he described the write-up of the Euler result), which he explained he had hurried out the door because he felt “pressured by outside factors.” The next day OpenAI issued their press release.

By Buckmaster’s account, he had reached out to OpenAI several days earlier, after word got back to him that rumors about his and Alpöge’s work were circulating there. He then, he said, had a tense back and forth with the company regarding how they had achieved their result and how they were going to announce it. Buckmaster had concerns that OpenAI had used work of his, which he had shared with the company by using its tools over the preceding months, never thinking that OpenAI was or would be working on Navier-Stokes. He alleged that in a phone call two days earlier an OpenAI scientist had offered him authorship on the company’s paper provided that Alpöge—an Anthropic employee—be left off. OpenAI denies trying to withhold credit from Alpöge (although it has said that it did want to bring only Buckmaster in as a coauthor). OpenAI also now claims that nothing Buckmaster typed could have reached the model. The company’s September 8 announcement credits both men, recognizes their priority on Euler, and says that it will not claim the prize. Whatever happened on that call, the episode cut against the oldest norms of scholarly credit and collaboration and fed the cynicism many of us already feel about the AI industry’s public professions of altruism.

Priority controversies are hardly new in academia, or in mathematics, for that matter, but there are greater stakes here. It is meaningful that the AI giants have chosen mathematics as the arena for a cage match. Mathematics is a touchstone of intelligence, even of genius, and there is no dispute about when a problem is solved. A problem that withstood generations of officially very smart people is, in this sense, the cleanest possible advertisement for a technology whose product is thinking. The machine that solved Navier-Stokes was not built to solve Navier-Stokes. That is the whole point of telling us that it did. What we are witnessing is a spectacle of computational power staged to acquire market share, and with it control of a landscape that extends well beyond mathematics.

OpenAI showed that the Navier-Stokes equations can “experience a singularity.” But did we? The model solved one of the world’s most important math problems. But it’s just a math problem. These are, for sure, complicated puzzles, some generated by thinking about the world around us and many that come completely from a world inside us, vistas on some elaborate ziggurat of the intellect that we continue to build. Solving them brings joy and understanding to a relatively small number of people around the world.

Unfortunately, the most important problems that we face are not math problems. Some, like climate change and even AI’s “alignment problem,” have mathematical components, but the most important problems are people problems, and no matter how much we might try to make them into math problems, they aren’t. Mathematicians have been solving longstanding math problems for centuries. If this were a sign of superintelligence, I’d like to think that at least one of these problem solvers could have brought more lasting happiness to the human race.

Did OpenAI’s model do math? Kind of. Mathematicians have been using machines to help prove theorems for over fifty years. Whatever the machine did here, however, it did not do it in the way humans would. One way to say what it did was that it “simulated” the act of doing mathematics—albeit to great effect. Any given piece of that scratch work might look like a dashed-off expression on a blackboard or an email between collaborators. And yet the process as a whole—a group of people serving up and organizing ideas for a machine—is, well, very un-mathlike.

For some problem-solvers, settling a question is perhaps the only point of pure mathematics. The focus on the goal makes professional mathematics seem like big-game hunting and the profession like a competition. That is at least part of what Buckmaster might have meant when he called OpenAI’s solution a “Deep Blue/Kasparov moment.” But there is also something about the human journey in mathematical research. For most of us the process is itself at least as important, even a source of pleasure in its own right: looking at delicate symbolic hieroglyphics, puzzling alone and with others over a complicated expression or idea, the simple satisfaction of thinking hard about something, turning it over purposely and unconsciously, marinating in a problem. Living with a problem. We talk to ourselves and we talk to others, and when everything finally falls into place we take our time to give a careful, bullet-proof explanation. A mathematics paper is a human activity, written, not generated. Asked why he had not used the new tools, Córdoba spoke for the collaboration that made the whole thing possible: “I don’t use AI. I have Luis.”

I am reminded of Walter Benjamin’s well-known essay “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction,” first drafted in 1935. It is a deep reflection on what the technologies of photography and especially filmmaking had done to the practice—the art—of image-making. In a deft rhetorical display he argues that, once mechanical reproduction untethers a work of art from its singular existence, society reaches a dialectical fork. On the one hand, photography and film can democratize image-making for all kinds of positive effects: good things can happen when everyone is an author, or even more, feels as though they can be an author. These technologies also “bring out those aspects of the original that are unattainable to the naked eye.” But with reproducibility “quantity has been transmuted into quality,” setting the stage for a battle between concentration and distraction. The result is to promote a public that, according to Benjamin, “is an examiner, but an absent-minded one.”

There is a political danger here as well. Ease of access, for Benjamin, is a form of sleight of hand—it gives the illusion of voice without transferring power or changing the structure of property ownership. This is a Marxist argument, which Benjamin wrote in the shadow of Nazism and the fascist takeover of Italy. At our historical remove much of it reads as prescient.

We are now confronted with machines that are able to produce things that we’ve historically viewed as works of thought. But do they reproduce thinking? The mapping of Benjamin’s argument onto such a question is not one-to-one, but the resonances are hard to miss. His central observation is that the technique of reproduction “detaches the reproduced object from the domain of tradition.” In its most quoted form this is the famous loss of “aura,” perhaps the essay’s best-known concept. It has nostalgic overtones but also points to new opportunity. With freedom comes possibility, art as a vehicle for political action.

We again stand at a historical juncture that threatens the “aura” of a long-standing human practice. One reading is that we are at a gateway to a period of rapid self-improvement and accelerated research, and soon to be released from traditional and increasingly irrelevant educational structures. Even proofs can now be certified by machines. Mathematicians—including Buckmaster and Alpöge—regularly advance their own research with AI tools.

But something has also been lost, and that loss cannot be taken lightly. Connected to the Greek word for “breath,” “aura” links to the body itself. Thought is human. “Aura” also speaks to the amazement that we should feel in the presence of creative work. Its loss suggests a marginalization of human activity and a disregard or even disrespect for the creative act. A proof only loosely attached to the people who spend their lives thinking becomes detached from the history of thought, and therefore from the foundation of meaning that it created. When a new technology untethers thoughts from their thinkers, we go from thinking for ourselves to thinking that we are thinking for ourselves. And because the aura has not disappeared but migrated, from the thinker to the machine, we are more inclined to believe what we are told, and ultimately to start valuing its “thoughts” more than our own.

Our thoughts are our own because they come from our cognitive processes, our biology, our history. No two thoughts are ever exactly the same. Now that so many of us pass our thoughts and ideas through a handful of common AI midwives, the many small singularities that were each of us collapse into a handful of larger ones. The wisdom of crowds becomes the wisdom of a few. Receiving the machine’s words in a room alone or wrapped up in headphones, we may experience them as our own ideas, but they aren’t. And the machines producing all those seemingly individual voices are owned by a very small number of powerful companies.

In the essay’s epilogue, Benjamin makes a direct connection to fascism. He reminds us of the Futurists and their celebration of the speed, power, and beauty of the machine. He quotes Marinetti, by then closely identified with Italian Fascism, extolling even modern warfare as an aesthetic triumph of technology. When speed and power become objects of admiration in themselves, the human activity they were supposed to serve becomes the slow thing, the obstacle. For Benjamin, writing in the interwar years, amid both memories of the technology-enabled carnage of World War I and the specter of fascism, the endpoint of that logic was war. Its’s not difficult to bring at least the first part of that analogy to OpenAI’s achievement: eighty-eight hours, ten thousand agents, 130 billion tokens, and one historic theorem. The announcement’s implicit message—intentional or not—is that humans are the past and LLMs are the future.

For Benjamin, this was a battle of aesthetics that ultimately played out on a real battlefield. Perhaps ours is also a battle of aesthetics that is now playing out in the environment, economy, and university. Whether we go on thinking for ourselves and with others—carefully and, yes, even slowly— when faster options are a click away is a choice. Sometimes the faster way is the better one. But sometimes you need Luis.

entries.title: A Plum Assignment
entries.summary: The cover for our Fall Books Issue—a painting of ripe purple plums in a punnet, surrounded by hand-painted cover lines—was an unexpected collaboration between the Irish-born New Yorker Lena Beug, a commercials director, and the Canadian Jason Logan, who makes ink from natural pigments that he forages from rural and urban environments. I had assigned the […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

The cover for our Fall Books Issue—a painting of ripe purple plums in a punnet, surrounded by hand-painted cover lines—was an unexpected collaboration between the Irish-born New Yorker Lena Beug, a commercials director, and the Canadian Jason Logan, who makes ink from natural pigments that he forages from rural and urban environments. 

I had assigned the fully illustrated cover to Logan, who was visiting New York at the end of August, and invited both Logan and Beug to dinner. While he was sketching ideas, she arrived bearing plums to cook the popular New York Times plum torte. The dinner table was covered in paint and paper, and Beug sat down and made some quick brush studies before starting to bake. After Logan’s first idea was rejected a few days later, he went back to the drawing board and made inky paintings of leaves and landscapes, hand lettering around the shapes. He then tossed one of Lena’s paintings into the ring. We agreed that it looked luscious. (The editors at first thought the punnet looked like a chair, but flipping the image solved the problem and the cover was decided.)

I wrote to Beug and Logan last week to ask them about art making, collaboration, and plums.

Leanne Shapton: Had you met before that afternoon in August?

Lena Beug: Never, but I have a tiny bottle of Jason’s ink on my tray of tiny, precious things. But we hadn’t met. I liked making a new friend.

Jason Logan: I feel like I have known Lena for years, but we just met that afternoon at your place.

Lena, you direct commercials for clients like eBay, Target, and Toyota, but what is your art-making practice like?

Beug: My practice is mostly just to make things, ideally without a lot of importance placed on the outcome. I have some complicated feelings about “Art” that may have something to do with being the child of a painter and having dropped out of art college, so it’s better if I just do it. I’m deep in a world of papier-mâché shells and pearls on my kitchen counter right now. I’m drawn to food and cute things like flowers and puppies and jewels and cake.

And Jason, what is yours?

Logan: I make ink from pigments I forage from sidewalks and wild spaces. My art is always a testing of the possibilities of the materials I combine. I particularly like hand lettering text, which is a place where word and image commingle.

Were any of the plums eaten before you painted the punnet?

Beug: Yes, at least one, I love plums.

Jason how was the plum cake?

Logan: The plum cake felt like that moment between summer and fall. A perfect meeting of sweet and tart, sticky and crumbly, light and rich, elegant and straightforward, with a dark plummy inside and a dusting of powdered sugar on top. Like an easy conversation with new friends.

I thought it was unusual, in this age of self-promotion and ruthless jockeying for attention, that I gave you, Jason, the assignment, but then you lobbied for trying someone else’s painting on the cover. Why?

Logan: I loved the look of the plums tucked into a basket. They felt right for the cover, itself an easy union of some of the best thinking and writing of the moment. The plums also embody something of the season, and of new friendships: playful painting at the end of the summer in a screened-in porch at a cottage on the water; pink wine and lobster rolls and yard-sale finds. The guilelessness of this leftover sketch on a scrap of paper won me over, beating out whatever needs I had for seeing my own artwork in the spotlight. I love what Lena made, I loved hand lettering around it with my favorite black walnut ink, and I loved working with Leanne, too. You always bring out the unexpected. The world has enough jockeying for attention, and not enough of whatever you might call this project.

Harmonizing?

Logan: Yeah.

Lena, your parents are longtime subscribers to the Review, what did they think of the cover?

Beug: The first thing I said when I found out about the cover decision was, “my parents will be delighted,” and they are.

You left your paintings behind after that dinner. Why didn’t you take any with you when you left? Were they still wet?

Beug: They weren’t wet, I just don’t need to keep everything. I like keeping it light. Also, as it turns out, if I had taken it with me, it probably wouldn’t have ended up on the cover.

entries.title: Lucy Sante on Pauline Kael, Film Criticism, and Pop Culture
entries.summary: In the second season premiere of Private Life, host Jarrett Earnest is joined by the writer and critic Lucy Sante to discuss Pauline Kael’s career, pop culture writing, and Sante’s writing for the Review, where she has been a frequent contributor since the 1980s. The conversation focuses on “The Perils of Pauline” (published in the […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In the second season premiere of Private Life, host Jarrett Earnest is joined by the writer and critic Lucy Sante to discuss Pauline Kael’s career, pop culture writing, and Sante’s writing for the Review, where she has been a frequent contributor since the 1980s. The conversation focuses on “The Perils of Pauline” (published in the magazine’s August 14, 1980, issue), Renata Adler’s blistering assessment of Kael’s film criticism; the legacy of staff film critics; and Sante’s relationship with popular music from Elvis to The Velvet Underground.  

Lucy Sante is the author of Low Life: Lures and Snares of Old New York (1991), Six Sermons for Bob Dylan (2024), and the memoir I Heard Her Call My Name (2024). Her first essay for the Review, “Relic” (published in the December 17, 1981, issue), reviewed Albert Goldman’s controversial 1981 biography, Elvis. Sante taught writing and the history of photography at Bard College for twenty-four years.

entries.title: Sand Castles
entries.summary: To begin, a guessing game. The February 1967 issue of Cahiers du cinéma includes a “Dictionary of New French Cinema” comprising capsule commentaries on 157 directors. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
To begin, a guessing game. The February 1967 issue of Cahiers du cinéma includes a “Dictionary of New French Cinema” comprising capsule commentaries on 157 directors. One of these offers the following superlative assessment: “She remains (now alongside Marguerite Duras) the greatest female auteur of our cinema.”

Naming the recipient of this praise shouldn’t be difficult, given the exceedingly few women active as directors in 1960s France. The New Wave was populated by rebellious sons casting off the cinéma de papa with oedipal gusto; it was a movement conjugated, to borrow Geneviève Sellier’s memorable formulation, in the “masculine singular.” So who could belong in the company of the grande dame Duras? Most will likely put their chips on Agnès Varda, who had made her debut feature La Pointe Courte ahead of the curve in 1954, earning her the dubious epithet of the “mother” of the New Wave—or even sometimes, in a generational stretch that likely owes much to the filmmaker’s carefully crafted later-life persona, its “grandmother.” But the answer is someone relatively few would recognize, a woman to whom film history has not been kind: Paula Delsol.

When Cahiers published its “Dictionary,” Delsol had written and directed only a single feature: La Dérive (1964), a fresh and dark story of an errant girl who drifts, as the title has it, from man to man. “Peppered with bold strokes halfway between recklessness and genius, the film baffled almost everyone at the time,” wrote the Cahiers editors. “Yet today, it is a work that makes one forget whatever else might have been attempted on the same subject.” This belated acclaim didn’t stick; La Dérive was largely omitted from the many stories subsequently told about one of the most combed-over quarters of world cinema. Even in Sellier’s Masculine Singular, a feminist book that sees the “central problematic” of the New Wave as “the relations between men and women and, more generally, the construction of sexual identities,” the film is consigned to a footnote, where it is deemed both “astonishing” and “invisible.” This June, when La Dérive screened to a full house at Bologna’s Il Cinema Ritrovato, a festival devoted to archival programming, the man introducing it asked for a show of hands from audience members who had seen it before, seemingly confident that the numbers would be low, even in such a cinephile crowd. As he had predicted, only a scattering of the hundreds of attendees were repeat viewers.

Forgotten, invisible: these adjectives have reliably accompanied La Dérive into the twenty-first century. But it seems that Delsol, who passed away in 2015, is finally getting her due. After a sprinkling of screenings in recent years and a trickle of scholarly attention, the Cinémathèque Française recently undertook a new 4k restoration of the film, which roughly coincided with the publication of a short monograph about it in French by the academic Aurore Renaut.* The restoration will show at this year’s London Film Festival and have its North American premiere at the New York Film Festival. Further circulation will follow: it has been acquired by Janus Films, the preeminent distributor of classic cinema, which shares an owner with the Criterion Collection. The institutional stamps of approval, in short, are piling up.

The reemergence of La Dérive is part of one of the most significant phenomena in contemporary film culture: an archive fever running high enough to inspire delirium. What has been called the post-Covid “repertory boom” in fact has little resemblance to the predigital practice of repertory programming, which amounted to the repeated exhibition of a set of tried-and-true classics. Driven by a desire to contest the false objectivity of the canon and a fatigue with the state of contemporary media, programmers and cinephiles are making increasingly deep forays into the cinema’s many histories. The age of revivalism has arrived, playing out in restoration-focused festivals, theatrical runs, specialized disc labels, little magazines like Narrow Margin, and online communities like Letterboxd. The editors of n+1 could have been writing about film when they recently proclaimed, “If the past few years of American literary publishing have had a zeitgeist, it has been more like a series of geists from zeits past.” When so much of contemporary culture feels familiar even before it is encountered, and when bloated tentpoles try to pass themselves off as the height of cinematic artistry by insisting on a 70mm release, bright shines the nugget that had previously fallen through the sieve.

Bringing underseen works into greater visibility can be not only politically important but flat-out thrilling—as the soaring attendance at recent editions of Cinema Ritrovato attests. And yet the restoration and circulation of historical films is part of an economy of money and attention, in which the assertion that a film is “forgotten” can feel less like the recognition of an injustice and more like a marketing tag. Many films simply aren’t as forgotten as they’re made out to be, while others came and went in their own time because they were, in a word, forgettable. The ratio between hype and quality is sometimes askew. But then there are rediscoveries like La Dérive, which fully justify the fanfare. Now what baffles is not the film itself, but how something so accomplished and so proximate to the French New Wave could remain so little known for so long.

Advertisement

Paula Delsol was born in 1923 in Montagnac, a town about an hour’s drive from Montpellier in southern France. Her given name—which appears in the credits of La Dérive—was Paule, but many called her Paula and she came to prefer the mistake. Like Duras, Delsol grew up in what was then French Indochina (now Vietnam), where members of her family had lived since the nineteenth century. She returned to France in 1946 and married a year later, only for the partnership to rapidly deteriorate. A single mother in need of work, she opened a beauty school in Montpellier in 1951 but by the middle of the decade was increasingly devoting herself to creative pursuits. In 1955 she published her first novel, Adieu et merci, a semi-autobiographical story of a young French colonial who returns to the metropole after the defeat at Dien Bien Phu.

Delsol had long been fascinated by cinema and had experimented with her father’s 8mm camera. In 1954 she worked as a volunteer assistant director on Denys Colomb de Daunant’s Glamador, where she met the cinematographer Jean Malige. That same year, with financial assistance from Delsol’s father the pair founded a film production facility, the Studio Auditorium du Languedoc, which came to be used by Parisian directors shooting in the region and led to Delsol working as a “script-girl” on François Truffaut’s Les Mistons (1958). She began to make short films with Malige, who became her second husband in 1958 and who would go on to shoot La Dérive. In a moment when French cinema was being transformed by pathbreaking debuts—not just Truffaut but Claude Chabrol, Jean-Luc Godard, Jacques Rivette, and Éric Rohmer all released their first features around the turn of the decade—Delsol, nearly ten years older than many of the New Wave luminaries, set out to take her place among them. Helped once more by an inheritance from her father as well as counsel from Truffaut, she embarked upon her first feature with limited resources and complete creative freedom, acting as her own producer. By early 1960 the script was finished and a casting call went out.

La Dérive has all the elliptical brio one would expect from the nouvelle vague—its editor, Agnès Guillemot, worked extensively with Godard—but is colored by desperation and attuned to the brutal, interlocking regimes of gender and class. “I wanted to make a portrait…of a young girl who wanted to escape from her environment,” said Delsol in a 1963 interview. “I wanted to show that women were looking to be the equal of men in terms of their sexual freedom, and that in playing that game they would always be beaten.” Her blonde protagonist, Jacquie (played by Jacqueline Vandal)—a character inspired by the working-class girls Delsol encountered at the beauty school—is a gorgeous dropout who has abandoned her hometown of Palavas-les-Flots, a fishing village south of Montpellier, with her musician boyfriend, Pierre. As La Dérive begins, they have been away for two years and Jacquie is hungry. Calling himself an “alley cat,” Pierre explains that he cannot give her what all girls desire, to be safe and warm, and suggests that if she wants to eat three times a day she should return home. “I’d rather die!” she exclaims. But soon Pierre slips away while Jacquie is napping on a train, and she has no choice but to set out on her own toward Palavas.

Life after Pierre involves meeting men in a noxious swirl of adventure and threat, with the whiff of money never far away. Jacquie accumulates sexual encounters, the particulars of which the film mostly elides with striking interludes of black. First there is a one-night stand with a medical intern who calls himself Jack the Ripper sooner than reveal his real identity; next a truck driver whom Jacquie, while hitchhiking, must burn with a cigarette to escape his unwanted advances. Then a wealthy nephew and uncle buy her favor, at least for a time. Finally, an artist in the dunes promises her love today but no guarantee of tomorrow. Returning to Palavas also means reencountering a former suitor, the kind fisherman Jean, who has chosen a simple life after his service in Algeria and who proposes marriage; her only real friend, he is the one prospect with whom she does not go to bed. Once again, she’d rather die.

Shooting on location, notably during the 1961 Feria de Pentecôte in Nîmes, Delsol filled her film with the faces of nonprofessionals and the documentary energies of place, mixing a realist impulse with the sharp edges of modernist fragmentation. In some scenes a hidden camera was used to capture life uninhibited. Like Varda’s La Pointe Courte—coincidentally or not, another work set in the south of France and funded at least in part by a family inheritance—La Dérive is distinctly a film of the Midi and, as such, a geographical outsider in a New Wave largely defined by Parisian urbanity. It is filled with open-air scenes and local color: sand dunes and village dances, fishing nets and bulls. Reentering this world, Jacquie—whom the town gossips mock for acting like a “dolled-up Parisian”—brings with her a shock of the modern, one that seems to ripple out from her person into the film’s form, corroding its naturalism. The opening sequence, in which credits repeatedly cut into a conversation between Jacquie and Pierre, establishes Delsol’s jagged style: she gives us a woman’s life in shard-like glimpses, a fitting treatment for a character who breaks with tradition and abandons herself to the present.

By 1963 it was time for Delsol to submit the completed film to the censors and obtain the certificate necessary for release. Here trouble began. “Owing to the profoundly immoral comportment of certain characters of the film,” La Dérive was restricted to audiences over eighteen. The decision had a disastrous impact on its commercial prospects: Gaumont withdrew its interest in distribution. “It’s incredible,” Delsol told a journalist from L’Express that same year, “if someone plots the death of another man throughout a whole film, that isn’t immoral, whereas a girl who does what she wants with her own body is shameful.” Ultimately, the film received a limited release from a small company in the dog days of August 1964, when most Parisians would be on holiday. Delsol called it “a failure”; it was not until 1977 that she succeeded in making her second feature film.

According to Renaut’s monograph, Delsol believed that two specific passages were responsible for the rating, both of which she refused to cut. The first pertains to a crucial detail of Jacquie’s backstory: she is infertile, a fact that both enables her sexual freedom in a pre-pill France and complicates her relation to normative femininity, which is to say motherhood. After a first casual mention to the intern, this information resurfaces in conversation with her friend Agathe. “I had a difficult pregnancy and so they operated on me,” Jacquie says, referring to her time with Pierre. “A difficult pregnancy” can mean many things, but one possibility was an abortion, which was illegal in France until 1975. (Delsol later said Jacquie was inspired by a woman who had undergone the procedure many times.)

The second offending scene occurs late in the film, after the wealthy uncle, Maurice, installs Jacquie in his seaside villa, where her mother comes to visit. The older woman is both impressed and concerned: “If I weren’t ashamed, I’d say you’re lucky,” she says to her daughter, before turning to practical matters. “Nothing here belongs to you, and yet you’re giving him your entire youth.” She advises Jacquie to make some kind of arrangement—presumably trading sex and companionship for money or property—to secure her future. A cynical, scheming mother: beyond the pale in the censors’ eyes. Jacquie, for her part, seems unconcerned. Before long she leaves Maurice to run along the seashore toward a new lover, replaying the ending of Truffaut’s The 400 Blows (1959) with a gendered twist.

Along with “invisible” and “forgotten,” there is a third adjective often appended to La Dérive, one that begins to explain why it fell into oblivion and why it is being resuscitated with enthusiasm today: feminist. Delsol distanced herself from the label. “If I wanted to serve the feminist movement, I would have participated in demonstrations,” she said in 1977, stating that she sought instead to make films about “women’s revolt.” But already in 1963, a critic writing for the leftist newspaper Combat proposed that the “essential quality” of La Dérive was “that it is the first deliberately ‘feminist’ film.” While “firsts” should be met with as much skepticism as declarations that a film was “forgotten,” there is no disputing that Delsol staked out new ground with her unjudgmental depiction of a promiscuous woman who rejects marriage, family, and employment alike.

This is not to suggest that La Dérive is a tale of empowerment. Jacquie moves through the film with fatalistic resignation, drifting from one episode to the next, seemingly open to anything that helps her forget Pierre and avoid what she is sure she does not want: a life like her poor, dowdy sister’s, the life she has been born into. While the intern’s assumed name raises the specter of sex work early in the film, it is Maurice who is most explicit about the transactional nature of their affair: “You’ll see how, for a woman, it’s nice to be bought. Since the world has existed, there have always been women who sell themselves and men to buy them.” When the alternative is to do worse and to do it for free, his proposal doesn’t seem so bad.

Through it all, however, Jacquie somehow never gives up on falling in love. When Agathe, a model for nude magazines, visits her in the château owned by Maurice’s playboy nephew, Régis, her canniness stands in stark contrast to Jacquie’s sentimentality. Jacquie may be a figure of defiance, but she also lacks education and opportunity, and readily buys into to the kinds of scenarios sold in cheap paperbacks and watched through tears at three-hanky matinées. Régis says she is “a bit dimwitted” and Maurice deems her part of a generation of “decadent romantics”; at the time of the film’s release, a male critic wrote in L’Aurore that she is “a brainless little twit who deserves a slap more than she does compassion.” And yet La Dérive never mocks her, never punishes her. It stays with her, pays attention to her—and attention is, as Simone Weil knew, “the rarest and purest form of generosity.”

Jacquie’s picaresque offers no arc of liberation, no coming to self-knowledge, no celebration of a woman’s “agency.” If anything, the film’s ending—in which Jacquie opts for a bohemian lover with no regard for the future—is a loop back to the start, an affirmation of the fleeting pleasures of a life lived in the present that also feels like a tightening of the noose. La Dérive has, in other words, few of the qualities often trotted out to laud a film as certifiably feminist. But Jacquie’s difficult return to village life, during which she never makes peace with the social role assigned to her, shows what happens when a young woman refuses to be bored, refuses to give in. Without shame, the film suggests how dead-ends, failures, and acts of self-sabotage are woven into the texture of a woman’s experience, and how a stubborn attachment to the dream of a different life can persist despite them all.

In her BFI Classics monograph on Barbara Loden’s Wanda (1970)—another work of women’s cinema belatedly heralded as a gem—the scholar Elena Gorfinkel describes Loden’s protagonist as “neither an affirmative nor a redemptive heroine,” arguing that “she represented a nascent feminist articulation of the problems, if not the solutions.” This holds true for Jacquie, as well. She figures as a sister not just to Wanda but also to Mona in Varda’s Vagabond (1985) and Firdaus in Nina Menkes’s Queen of Diamonds (1991): across decades, they form a sorority of women who refuse the safety of the home and choose an impossible revolt, one no less profound for at times being indistinguishable from self-destruction.These are films that brim with ambivalence and dare to stray, and whose characters show no hint of the imperative of self-optimization ubiquitous today. This is surely why, more than in their own time, they have proven especially attractive of late, when so many promises of feminist empowerment have soured, been coopted, or simply come to naught, but so many problems remain.

It should come as no surprise that women’s filmmaking, long marginalized and devalued, has been a signal part of the recent mania for peering into the dimmer corners of film history. For forty years there were no books on Wanda and now there are three; one can happily assume that discussion of La Dérive is about to surge. Restoration is an important step in generating this kind of interest, which in turn transforms a film’s position in history. Unlike an out-of-print book, which can be purchased online or accessed in a library, a 35mm film print sitting on a shelf will remain invisible to the public unless a professional takes the initiative to project it or digitize it. Without the archivists, restorationists, and curators who labor to bring lesser-known titles to audiences—first at festivals and eventually via home-viewing—vast swaths of film history will go unseen and the exclusions that have prevailed for so long will persist. But as the old is made new again, it is only more pressing to trace the shape of disappearance, to jolt the notion of the “forgotten film” out of the passive voice. In some instances, the same institutions and publications today so concerned with revival are the ones that had previously consigned those works to oblivion, however unwittingly. Papering over these acts of negligence has the effect of obscuring historical conditions of circulation and reception, depriving us of a chance to understand how the dominant picture of twentieth-century cinema that we have today first came into focus.

La Dérive was forgotten. Why? According to the Cinémathèque Française, it was the censors’ rating that “prematurely sealed the cinematic fate of its creator.” But misogyny undoubtedly played a part; in a 1964 Cahiers review, Louis Marcorelles noted that the film “speaks of love with such frankness that a good number of men are angered by it.” La Dérive also is an ill-fit with two major canon-building paradigms, the first of which is auteurism. The film was not Delsol’s sole outing; she went on to make a range of shorts (including the intriguingly titled Mille et un sexes, a documentary from 1974 in which people discuss gender identity), programs for television, and eventually the feature film Ben et Bénédict (1977), starring Françoise Lebrun of The Mother and the Whore (1973), which one can only hope will be restored soon. And yet in a film culture that valorizes directors by tracing a stylistic signature across a large body of work—an approach invented by the Young Turks of the New Wave that continues strong today—Delsol remains inassimilable: she simply did not make enough features. This makes her work less likely to be programmed by cinémathèques which have long devoted significant resources to single-author retrospectives.

The film also defies some expectations of feminist film culture. Jacquie’s willingness to make herself an object of male use and Delsol’s resistance to being identified as a feminist likely lessened its chances of being embraced by writers and curators who endeavored to rewrite film history in a feminine key from the early 1970s onward. Perhaps they just didn’t know about Delsol. But the atmosphere of resignation and ensnarement that pervades La Dérive may leave a bad taste for those who prefer their films sweet with the flavor of women’s independence and self-actualization.

Delsol’s working title for La Dérive was “Sand Castles,” a nod to both its littoral setting and the fragility of Jacquie’s liaisons and dreams. For decades, this could also have been a way of describing her debut: a delicate film washed away by a wave of Truffauts, Godards, and Chabrols. But it is the title that the director ultimately chose that offers a better allegory of what La Dérive teaches: swept in on the tide after decades adrift, it comes bearing lessons about the small-minded forces that first pushed it out to sea.
